- Upon reviewing the previous experiments, I observe that Run 1 (S=1.0, cat=0.05) and Run 2 (S=3.0, cat=0.15) both maintained an identical Substrate-to-Catalyst ratio (S/cat = 20). Because this ratio was constant, many models could simply scale their rate constants to fit both curves, maintaining the steady-state approximation. My aim to strongly perturb the system was only partially achieved because the relative stoichiometry remained unchanged.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To break this degeneracy, we must drastically alter the S/cat ratio and push the system out of the steady-state (Michaelis-Menten) regime. 
I propose an experiment with a very low substrate concentration (S=0.5) and the maximum allowable catalyst concentration (cat=0.20), yielding an S/cat ratio of 2.5. 
1. In this regime, a significant fraction of the total substrate will be rapidly bound into the `catS` complex. This will strongly differentiate mechanisms that depend on free `cat` (e.g., M2, M9, M13) from those that depend on the `catS` complex (e.g., M14, M18), because the transient dynamics of `cat` vs `catS` will be vastly different than in the S >> cat regime.
2. By using the maximum catalyst concentration (0.20), we will maximize the rate of any second-order catalyst interactions (M2, M13, M18, M19), creating a massive divergence between first-order and second-order catalyst models.
3. Setting initial product to 0.0 ensures we cleanly observe the pre-steady-state burst kinetics and catalyst sequestration effects without interference from product-binding or product-deactivation, isolating the S/cat interaction dynamics.
</hypothesis>
